task_description: Translate the given Punjabi sentence into natural, idiomatic English. Correct translation requires understanding idioms and pragmatic meaning, not just literal word mapping.

scripts.latin: surinder di salah leh ke na baithna uh tah kath da ullu hai

reference_translation.text: Don’t take Surinder’s advice; he’s completely foolish.

items.notes: ‘Kath da ullu’ is an idiom meaning extremely foolish, not literally an owl made of wood.

scripts.latin: jado ohdh pohdh karn naal mera pet thik nhi hoya, tan mainu hospital le gye

reference_translation.text: When home remedies didn’t fix my stomach problem, they took me to the hospital.

items.notes: ‘Odh pohdh’ refers to home remedies or informal treatment.

scripts.latin: ladai de dina vich har cheez agg de bah vikdi hai

reference_translation.text: During times of conflict, everything sells at extreme prices.

items.notes: Metaphorical use of ‘agg de bah’ conveys economic chaos and price exploitation.

scripts.latin: bharat vich majbi januni saiyappe di nain hai

reference_translation.text: In India, religious extremism is the main root of all problems.

items.notes: ‘Majbi januni’ conveys religious extremism rather than general religiosity.

scripts.latin: hadd haram naukar kite vi nhi tik sakde

reference_translation.text: Extremely lazy workers can’t last anywhere.

items.notes: ‘Hadd haram’ implies chronic laziness or work-shyness, not dishonesty.

scripts.latin: jabani jamah kharch karn di tha asli kamm karna chahida hai

reference_translation.text: Instead of making half-hearted attempts, one should do real work.

items.notes: The phrase criticizes weak or performative effort, not literal speech.

scripts.latin: Ma ne kudi nu jappi paake keha, “Marjaaniye, kithe reh gayi si tu? Sara din teri fikar kardi pyi si.”

reference_translation.text: Hugging her daughter, the mother said, “Where did you disappear to, you silly girl? I've been worried about you all day.”

items.notes: ‘Marjaaniye’ is literally a curse (roughly ‘you who should die’) but functions as affectionate scolding. A literal rendering turns an embrace into abuse; the hug and the expressed worry license the warm register.

scripts.latin: Munde ne fer glass tod ditta te bebe ne keha, “Jeonda reh mere sher, ajj taan tu kamaal hi kar ditta.”

reference_translation.text: When the boy broke yet another glass, his grandmother said, “Well done, my little lion — you've really outdone yourself today.”

items.notes: ‘Jeonda reh’ is a blessing form deployed sarcastically. Every word is positive, so a literal translation yields sincere praise and loses the rebuke. Mirrors pa_tr_007: same polarity-inversion mechanism, opposite direction.

scripts.latin: Mez te das cheezan chun ke mezbaan ne keha, “Lo ji, kuch khaas nahi banaya, bas roti-paani hi hai.”

reference_translation.text: Having laid out ten dishes on the table, the host said, “Please eat — I haven't made anything special, just a simple meal.”

items.notes: Conventional host modesty: the disclaimer is ritual, not a factual description. The apparent contradiction with the ten dishes is the point and must survive translation — a translation that softens the spread or reads the host as genuinely apologetic destroys the implicature.

scripts.latin: Gawandan ne munde nu vekh ke keha, “Hai, kinna sohna lagda hai, nazar na lage.”

reference_translation.text: Looking at the boy, the neighbour said, “Oh, he looks so handsome — touch wood.”

items.notes: ‘Nazar na lage’ literally means ‘may the (evil) eye not fall on him’ and is an near-obligatory protective addition when praising a child. Omitting it loses meaning; translating it word-for-word produces something opaque in English. Requires a functional equivalent such as ‘touch wood’ / ‘bless him’.
